study.title: Psalms 118 - Thanksgiving, trust, and the rejected stone that God exalted
study.overview: Psalm 118 is a hymn of gratitude that opens and closes with the same call: thank the LORD because he is good and because his goodness endures forever. Throughout the poem, the psalmist passes from anguish to security, from the encircled by the enemies to the public celebration, and from the discipline received to the confession that God saved him. The psalm also extends the individual focus for the people of the covenant, calling Israel, the house of Aaron, and all who fear the LORD. At the center of the composition appears the great turning: the stone rejected by the builders becomes the main stone, which Christian commentators understand as a messianic reference applied to Jesus.

outline.title: Collective Invitation to Gratitude
outline.explanation: The psalm begins and ends with praise, and at first calls three groups to witness the same truth: Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the LORD. The idea is that the whole community of the covenant recognizes the constant goodness of God.

outline.title: From anguish to trust and victory
outline.explanation: The psalmist tells his experience: he cried in anguish, was heard, he received room to breathe and found that it is better to trust the LORD than in people or princes. Though surrounded and pressured, he claims that God helped him, corrected him without giving him to death and gave him reason to sing and tell the divine works.

outline.title: Admission thankful and the day that the Lord made
outline.explanation: He asks for access to the gates of justice to enter and praise. He then proclaims that the rejected stone became the main one, recognizing in this the wonderful action of the LORD. The result is joy: this is the day when God acted.

outline.title: Final cry, blessing and closing in praise
outline.explanation: The psalm asks for salvation and prosperity, blesses the one who comes in the name of the Lord, confesses the Lord as the true God who gave light and ends just as he began: with thanksgiving for God's permanent goodness.

study.context: The notes indicate that this psalm is the last of the Psalms of the Egyptian Hallel, that is, of the set of praises used in the celebration. There also appear signs of liturgical use in the temple, with mention at the gates, the priests and the altar. It is not safe to go beyond what the text and the notes say; but the psalm clearly sounds like a public thanksgiving, linked to community worship.
study.theology: The psalm teaches, first, that the goodness of God is stable and worthy of repeated praise, not only in moments of victory, but also in the midst of discipline. Second, the right trust opposes dependence on human power: even strong leaders are not a sure foundation for salvation. Third, the suffering of the righteous is not denied; it is reinterpreted in the light of the divine help, which corrects without destroying. Fourth, the image of the rejected stone points to the paradoxical way as God exalts what men despise. In the Christian reading presented by the commentators, this is especially fulfilled in Jesus, the rejected that becomes the main stone. Finally, the psalm holds together personal redemption, community joy and liturgical worship: the deliverance received leads to the public proclamation of the greatness of God.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm concludes the Egyptian Hallel and summons the whole community to witness the permanent goodness of the Lord, represented by Israel, the house of Aaron and those who fear the LORD.
The psalmist celebrates the mercy of God and invites others to recognize this goodness, which must be remembered and proclaimed.
Trusting in the Lord is better than trusting princes, because high-ranking people may not help and are not able to act in what belongs to salvation.

questions: In what situations have I sought more in human resources than in the Lord?
How can the discipline of God be received without being confused with abandonment?
How does the image of the rejected stone challenge my way of evaluating people and works of God?
study.practice: This week, choose a concrete area of pressure - family, work, finance or health - and turn anxiety into prayer as in verse 5. Then write two practical actions of trust: one that reduces its dependence on merely human solutions and the other that expresses public gratitude to God. It is also worth reciting the chorus of the psalm at the beginning and end of the day, as a discipline of spiritual memory: thank the LORD because he is good and his goodness endures forever.
study.uncertainty: Notes do not provide accurate historical data on original authorship, date or occasion, so you don't want to treat this information as secure. The connection of the psalm with Jesus, especially in verses 22 and 26, comes from the aforementioned interpretations and the use of the New Testament, therefore should be presented as a Christian reading and not as a conclusion imposed only by the text of the psalm. The exact sense of some liturgical images, such as gates of justice and to tie the sacrifices to the horns of the altar, remains partially open because the notes are brief.
